# 5.1 - Samples, Studies, and Bias {.unnumbered}

A radio station asks listeners to call in: *Should school start later?* 90% of the callers say yes.

Does that mean 90% of all students agree? Not necessarily. The people who called in chose to call. They may care much more than other students.

In this lesson, you learn who is in a study, what kind of study it is, and how {{< glink bias >}} can make the results wrong.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I name the population and the sample in a study.
- [ ] I tell a sample survey, an observational study, and an experiment apart.
- [ ] I name the type of bias in a sample or a question.
- [ ] I decide if results can be generalized to a population.
:::

{{< learn >}}

### 5.1.1 - Population and Sample

| | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Population** | The **whole group** we want to learn about. | All 1,200 students at a school. |
| **Sample** | The part of the population we collect data from. | 100 of those students. |

We can only {{< glink generalize >}} (say the results are true for the whole population) if the sample represents the population well.

***

### 5.1.2 - Three Types of Studies

| Type | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Sample survey** | Ask a sample questions. | Ask 100 students how many hours they sleep. |
| **Observational study** | Watch or measure. Do **not** change anything. | Compare the grades of students who do and do not play sports. |
| **Experiment** | **Do something** to the subjects (a treatment) and measure what happens. | Give half the students a 10-minute break before a test. Compare scores. |

:::{.you-try title="A scientist records how much soda people drink and their weight. What type of study is it?"}
An **observational study**. The scientist measures, but does not tell anyone how much soda to drink.
:::

***

### 5.1.3 - Bias

{{< glink bias text="Bias" >}} is when the way we collect data favors some answers. A biased sample does not represent the population.

| Type of bias | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Voluntary response | People choose if they answer. People with strong feelings answer most. | The radio call-in poll. |
| Convenience | The sample is whoever is easy to reach. | Asking only your friends. |
| Undercoverage | Some groups are left out of the sample. | Calling only home phones. Many people do not have one. |
| Nonresponse | People who were chosen do not answer. | Half of the mailed surveys never come back. |
| Response | The question or the setting pushes people to answer a certain way. | "Don't you agree that our great principal deserves a raise?" |

:::{.gotcha title="A bigger sample does not fix bias"}
A call-in poll with 10,000 callers is still biased. More people who chose to call does not make the sample represent everyone.
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Populations, Samples, and Studies**

1. Name the population and the sample.

   a. A city wants to know how residents feel about a new park. It surveys 400 residents.

   b. A farmer tests 50 apples from her orchard to check for worms.

   c. A school picks 30 seniors to ask about graduation plans.

2. Is each study a sample survey, an observational study, or an experiment? Explain.

   a. Researchers ask 500 adults how many hours of TV they watch.

   b. A coach has half the team stretch before practice and half not stretch. She counts injuries.

   c. A scientist records the weights of babies whose mothers smoked and babies whose mothers did not.

   d. Students give one plant fertilizer and another plant only water. They measure growth.

***

**Bias**

3. Name the type of bias. Explain how it could change the results.

   a. A website asks visitors to vote on their favorite phone.

   b. To learn about cafeteria food, a student asks people standing in the lunch line.

   c. A survey about internet use is done only on the internet.

   d. A survey asks, "Do you agree that dangerous skateboarding should be banned from parks?"

4. To find the favorite sport of students at a school, Jamal surveys 60 fans at a basketball game. Can he generalize his results to all students at the school? Explain.

5. Rewrite this question so it does not push people toward an answer: "Don't you think the school day is too long?"
